newsitem.title: FRANCE: Major surprised if anything like 12 pass EMU test.
newsitem.headline: Major surprised if anything like 12 pass EMU test.

text.p: British Prime Minister John Major said on Friday he would be surprised at anything like 12 countries qualifying for European monetary union in 1999 if the Maastricht treaty were interpreted strictly.

He had been asked about European Commission forecasts made on Wednesday that 12 countries -- excluding Britain, Italy and Greece -- would meet a Maastricht treaty requirement that public deficits be cut to three percent of Gross Domestic Product.

"I personally would be surprised if by January 1, 1999 anything remotely like 12 nations qualify for EMU on anything like a strict interpretaion of the criteria," he told a news conference at the end of a Franco-British summit here.

"If the criteria are interpreted liberally then of course more countries will qualify. If they are interpreted strictly then I would be very surprised, if when we get there, there are anything like that number," Major said after his talks with French President Jacques Chirac.

He noted there were other criteria besides the one on public deficits. The Maastricht treaty requires countries to reduce their debt to 60 percent of GDP and also sets standards on inflation, interest rates and currency stability.

"There are a range of other particular criteria where some countries are wildly outside the criteria. There are some countries on the debt criteria that are nearly 100 percent above the criteria with no credible likelihood that they are going to get down within it for a very long time," he said.

Debate on how many countries are likely to join EMU in 1999 is increasingly dominating the agenda in Europe after Spain, Portugal and Italy launched a last-minute dash in September to get their economies ready in time to be in from the start.

Many economists had expected these Mediterranean countries to join at a later stage and say Germany would prefer a smaller euro zone of rich northern European states at the start to ensure the new euro is as stable as the mark.
Chirac, however, at a Franco-Spanish summit earlier this week, lifted the hopes of Madrid and Rome by saying he was sure Spain would join in 1999, and hoped Italy would do so too.
Europe is to decide in early 1998 -- on the basis of 1997 fiscal and monetary performances -- which countries will join Economic and Monetary Union at its launch.
Major said Britain was moving towards meeting the Maastricht treaty criteria and this would allow it to decide nearer the time whether to join the single currency.
"I believe that Britain is moving very rapidly toward the criteria, where it would have the option of joining or not joining according to the way it decided at the time," he said.
Neither France nor Britain however changed their views on European monetary union during their two-day summit in Bordeaux.
"Things have not moved," Chirac told the news conference.
France has long said that the more countries that join monetary union the better.
